lesson_title: Moth-Sized Waves: How Bats, Ships and Hospitals See With Sound
hook_text: A bat can catch a moth in total darkness. Its secret is a wave exactly five millimetres long.
clip_script: Total darkness. A bat is hunting a moth it cannot see — and it catches it. How? The bat squeaks at 68 thousand hertz, far above anything you can hear. Do the division: 340 metres per second of sound, split into 68 thousand vibrations, gives waves just five millimetres long. Moth-sized waves. And that is the secret — waves slide around anything smaller than themselves, but they SLAP off anything their own size. To a five-millimetre wave, a moth is a wall. The squeak bounces back, the bat times it: one hundredth of a second means a round trip of 3,4 metres — halve it, moth at 1,7 metres, strike. Ships do the same trick with sonar to map the seabed a kilometre down. And hospitals do it through skin: ultrasound clicks echo off every layer inside the body, each echo timed to millionths of a second, and the timings become a picture of a baby — safely, because sound is not radiation. One equation, one halving, and suddenly sound is a way of seeing.
visual_style: A dark sky where a bat's squeak spreads as glowing rings that shatter off a moth; the scene dives underwater for a sonar ping to the seabed, then through skin into a softly lit ultrasound scan; the division 340 over 68 000 hangs in the air.
mood: Nocturnal wonder resolving into crisp arithmetic.
pacing: Hushed hunt, sharp echo snap, quick dive from sky to sea to hospital, calm landing on the safe-scan close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to see with your ears.
